title: Laurens Hammond: The Non-Musical Genius Who Changed Popular Music
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck profile Laurens "Larry" Hammond, the Evanston-born inventor who built the Hammond organ (notably the B3) and earlier inventions including the tickless clock, a synchronous-motor-based 3D film system (Teleview) and the shadowgraph stage effect, the automatic bridge table, and later the Novachord. They cover his education and early life, the 60-cycle synchronous motor, predecessors Hermann von Helmholtz and Thaddeus Cahill's Telharmonium, the tone wheel and drawbar design, marketing to churches and stations, the 1937 blind listening test against the FTC complaint from pipe organ makers, the Leslie speaker rivalry, and the company's later history under CBS, Suzuki, and the XK3 revival. The episode closes with a listener correction about PFAS removal from water.
topics: FTC pipe organ blind listening test

segments.title: Orlando tour date announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce the rescheduled Orlando live show on Friday, September 8, and direct listeners to the on-tour page for tickets.

segments.title: Introduction to Laurens Hammond
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on Larry Hammond, inventor of the electric Hammond organ, noting his name spelling and the confusion with John Hammond from Jurassic Park.

segments.title: Hammond's impact on rock and jazz
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Hammond B3's role in rock, jazz and pop songs, and note Hammond was tone deaf and never played an instrument.

segments.title: Hammond's childhood and education
segments.summary: Hammond was born in 1895 near Evanston, Illinois, to a banker father who died when he was two and an artist mother, and the family lived in Europe. As a boy he tinkered with engines, went to Cornell, and was a family of accomplished women.

segments.title: Becoming an independent inventor
segments.summary: After a drunken exam-day mistake at Cornell, Hammond decided to become an independent inventor. After World War One he worked as chief engineer at the Gray Motor Company, then struck out on his own and created a tickless clock.

segments.title: Synchronous motor and 60-cycle current
segments.summary: Hammond's synchronous motor used the precise 60-cycle alternating current adopted in the US, enabling precise electric clocks and other devices.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the explanation of the 3D film system.

segments.title: Teleview 3D films and shadowgraph
segments.summary: Hammond developed Teleview, a 3D film system using two cameras, synchronized shutter glasses, and a projection system; audiences found it too realistic. He then made the colored-lens shadowgraph effect used in the Ziegfeld Follies.

segments.title: Precursors: Cahill and Helmholtz
segments.summary: The hosts cover Hermann von Helmholtz's 1860s charting of harmonics and Thaddeus Cahill's Telharmonium, the first electromechanical instrument.

segments.title: Tone wheels and the Telharmonium's size
segments.summary: Explanation of the tone wheel mechanism, with the Telharmonium weighing about 200 tons and costing a large sum. Hammond shrank the tone wheel to a practical size.

segments.title: From clocks to the organ
segments.summary: As electric clocks became common, Hammond's company struggled. An assistant treasurer and church organist urged him to build an organ, and the team of Hammond and John Hanert used ninety-one tone wheels to reproduce pipe organ sounds. The company had also sold an automatic bridge table.

segments.title: Drawbars and tonal variations
segments.summary: Hammond's organ used electronic switches and tone bars instead of pipe stops, letting players create their own sounds, with a figure of 253 million possible tonal variations.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of early Hammond organ sales.

segments.title: Early sales and adoption
segments.summary: Hammond organs sold about 1,400 in the first year at roughly $1,250 and were marketed to churches and serious musicians. George Gershwin is said to have bought the first one. Churches, baseball stadiums and radio soap operas adopted them.

segments.title: FTC complaint and 1937 blind listening test
segments.summary: Pipe organ makers complained to the FTC about Hammond's ad claims. Hammond proposed a blind listening test at the University of Chicago Chapel in 1937, in which listeners often could not tell the instruments apart. The FTC then allowed claims that the organ sounded real and produced beautiful music, but not that it replicated a $10,000 pipe organ.

segments.title: Tangents on famous Grammy moments and Joe the Plumber
segments.summary: The hosts briefly digress on Joe the Plumber and a Grammy stage-rush incident involving Bob Newhart.

segments.title: Ethel Smith and Jimmy Smith
segments.summary: Ethel Smith popularized the Hammond organ with 'Tico Tico' in the film Bathing Beauty. Jimmy Smith, a jazz organist unrelated to her, took the instrument further.

segments.title: Leslie speaker and the rivalry with Don Leslie
segments.summary: The Leslie speaker's rotating horns and variable speed create vibrato that helps the organ sound. Don Leslie offered it to Hammond, who rejected it and tried to block its use with dealers, though dealers used it secretly.

segments.title: Later inventions and company history
segments.summary: Hammond's Novachord, the company's sales to CBS, Suzuki's purchase, and the 2002 XK3 revival. The hosts also discuss a future episode on Robert Moog.

segments.title: Listener correction on PFAS
segments.summary: A listener, Whitney B, corrects an earlier episode on zenobiotics, noting granular activated carbon and reverse osmosis remove PFAS from water.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and credit iHeartRadio.
